Where Two or Three Are Gathered
whair TOO or THREE ar GATH-erd
n. phr. (Christ's promise of His presence with the assembly that acts in His name)
Greek hou gar eisin duo ē treis synēgmenoi eis to emon onoma — synagō in the perfect passive participle, having been gathered together; eis to emon onoma, into or unto My name, which is more than a label spoken over a meeting.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

“For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” The promise is immense and its context is specific. It stands at the end of the Lord's instruction on discipline in the church: a brother is told his fault privately, then before two or three witnesses, then before the congregation; what the church binds on earth is bound in heaven; and the two or three who agree in asking are promised that it shall be done for them. The two or three are therefore not a minimum quorum for feeling God near but the witnesses and the assembly of Matthew's own paragraph, acting under Christ's authority in His name. Rightly read, the verse is one of the great texts for the local church. A small congregation discharging the Lord's own order has Christ in the midst of it — not less of Him than a multitude would have, for He is not divided by numbers — and the authority behind its discipline is heaven's. The baptist and congregational tradition has rested much here, and justly: the gathered church is Christ's institution and His presence is promised to it, which is why the apostle can speak of the power of our Lord Jesus Christ being present when the church is come together.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Gather, to bring together; to collect a number of separate things. Name, in Scripture, the authority or character of a person. Where two or three are gathered together in my name, Matthew 18:20, Christ's promise to the assembly acting under His authority.

expand to see more

Gather, to bring together; to collect individuals into one body or place.

Name, in Scripture, the authority, character, or revealed person of one named.

Greek synagō, to gather together, whence synagogue, an assembly.

Greek eis to emon onoma, unto my name — by His authority, not merely with mention of it.

Set at the close of the rule for church discipline, Matthew 18:15-20.

Key Scripture

Mat 18:20 — "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."

Mat 18:19 — "Again I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven."

Mat 18:17 — "And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican."

Heb 10:25 — "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."

Modern Corruption

The promise is detached from the church and its discipline and made a guarantee attaching to any small gathering, which is then used to argue that no congregation is needed at all.

expand to see more

The modern use of the verse is almost always as an assurance to a handful of friends that Christ is present wherever a few meet — and from there to the conclusion that formal church membership, ordinances, officers and discipline are optional extras for people who like institutions. Matthew 18 gives the words a precise home. They close a passage about telling a brother his fault, about witnesses, about the judgment of the church, and about binding and loosing; the two or three are the witnesses and the assembly of that very procedure. A text about the authority of the gathered church cannot be made an argument for dispensing with it.

The second misuse treats the words as a promise of felt presence proportioned to numbers, so that a small meeting must reassure itself. Christ's presence is not quantitative and the verse does not compare crowds. The principle to recover is the one the Reformed and baptist confessions draw out: the Lord Jesus is in the midst of His gathered people by His Spirit, so that a small congregation faithfully keeping His order lacks nothing of His authority — and, by the same token, the assembly that acts in His name must actually act in it, since the promise is to those gathered unto His name and not merely in His general vicinity.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek synagō, to gather, root of synagogue; eis to emon onoma, unto My name, that is, by His authority — set within the rule of church discipline.

expand to see more

Greek synagō (perfect passive), having been gathered together.

Greek duo ē treis, two or three — the witnesses of Matthew 18:16.

Greek onoma, name, standing for the authority and person named.

Greek en mesōi autōn, in the midst of them, of Christ's own presence.

Preceded by binding and loosing and the judgment of the church, Matthew 18:17-18.

Usage

"where two or three are gathered together in my name"

"there am I in the midst of them"

"tell it unto the church"
